children: Successful webhook implementations will naturally evolve with improvements in messaging, new features, and better security controls. Webhook providers — such as

content.name: p
children: is an example of a provider that changed versions of its webhook notification over the years. In its initial version (v1), Hubspot signed only the webhook request body to validate calls. Over the years, Hubspot improved its webhooks to include timestamp validation, changed the webhook signature contents, and changed the encoding from hex to base64.

content.name: p
children: By informing the webhook signature version to the listener (via a header value or within the signed message), Hubspot made forward compatibility possible without breaking legacy endpoints. The versioning also allowed Hubspot to rollout webhook improvements per event basis, reducing the migration complexity for both provider and consumers.

content.name: p
children: Versioned schemes also protect against downgrade attacks.
tells consumers to ignore every scheme other than
signature it adds to test events — so an attacker can't strip the strong signature and leave a weaker one.

content.name: p
children: Signatures are only half of the contract; the payload changes too. Two approaches stand out:

children.name: li
strong
children: Pin the payload to an API version.

Stripe structures snapshot events according to the API version of the account or endpoint when the event is created, so upgrading the API doesn't change the shape of events an existing endpoint receives until the endpoint is upgraded.

children.name: li
strong
children: Don't version the payload at all.
carry only IDs, and the consumer fetches the object through an API version it controls. Stripe notes this makes integrations easier to maintain because the payloads are unversioned.
